landscape: Measures of political regimes are heavily used in comparative politics, and the field has moved through three generations. The first generation, from the 1970s to the 1990s, consisted of single-author or small-team indices built from expert judgment or a few observable indicators: Polity, Freedom House, Vanhanen, Bollen, Arat, Gasiorowski and Hadenius. Most of these are now frozen and survive mainly through replication archives and the democracyData R package. The second generation, from about 2000 to 2015, brought explicit decision rules for binary classifications (Cheibub-Gandhi-Vreeland, Boix-Miller-Rosato, LIED) and typologies of autocracy (Geddes-Wright-Frantz, Hadenius-Teorell-Wahman). It also brought the first attempts to model measurement error by pooling existing indices, as the Unified Democracy Scores did. The third generation is dominated by Varieties of Democracy, which collects disaggregated expert ratings, aggregates them with Bayesian item-response models and publishes uncertainty intervals and annual versioned releases. A growing family of derived products (Regimes of the World, Episodes of Regime Transformation, the State Capacity Index of O'Reilly and Murphy) builds directly on V-Dem.

Governance, corruption and state capacity form a second cluster. It is dominated by composite perception indices from international organisations and NGOs, chiefly the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators and Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index. Commercial country-risk ratings feed into these composites, the International Country Risk Guide above all. Academic alternatives have appeared in the last decade. They include Bayesian latent measures with uncertainty (the Bayesian Corruption Indicator, Hanson-Sigman state capacity), objective indicators of informational capacity and legibility (the Information Capacity Dataset, Myers-score data), and procurement-based corruption-risk indicators. Practically every regime and governance measure is redistributed in the Quality of Government Standard dataset, which is often the most convenient point of access.

Of the 98 REG rows in the catalog, 40 are frozen, 7 discontinued and 3 superseded, which reflects how many influential measures have stopped updating. Polity5 ends in 2018; Unified Democracy Scores in 2012; Geddes-Wright-Frantz in 2010; Freedom House's Nations in Transit published its final edition in 2024. Researchers who need data past these end points should move to an actively maintained successor rather than extending an old series by hand.

core.text: V-Dem is widely used in contemporary regime research. It provides hundreds of indicators coded by country experts and aggregates them into five high-level democracy indices (electoral, liberal, participatory, deliberative, egalitarian), together with accountability, corruption and civil-liberties indices. Latent scores come from a Bayesian ordinal item-response model that adjusts for differences in how coders use the scales, and every estimate carries a credible interval. Coverage runs from 1789 to 2025 in the v16 release, with yearly updates. Its main weakness is shared with all expert-coded data: possible time-varying coder bias, debated in the exchange between Little and Meng (2024) and Knutsen et al. (2024). Pin the version you use, because scores are revised retroactively.

Polity remains heavily cited, mostly in its Polity IV form. Its 21-point polity score combines coded authority characteristics: executive recruitment, constraints on the executive and political competition. The series ends in 2018 and the project is frozen. Users should know the published critiques. Gleditsch and Ward (1997) show that the scale is driven largely by executive constraints, and Vreeland (2008) shows that its middle range partly codes political violence, which matters for civil-war research. Use it for replication, for very long series and for comparison with older work; prefer V-Dem or LIED for new analyses after 2018.

Freedom in the World rates political rights and civil liberties annually for all countries and many territories from the 1973 edition onward, with indicator-level subscores from 2003. It measures the freedoms people actually enjoy rather than formal institutions, so it is well suited to questions about rights but conflates regime type with repression outcomes. Bollen and Paxton (2000) and Steiner (2016) document rater-specific error and possible political bias. Current data are released through a request form rather than as an open download.

The Boix-Miller-Rosato coding is a widely used dichotomous measure that covers the nineteenth century. It classifies country-years from 1800 to 2020 as democratic when leaders are chosen in free and fair elections and a minimum share of men (or adults) can vote. It complements the Cheibub-Gandhi-Vreeland/Bjørnskov-Rode family, which applies an alternation rule instead of a suffrage threshold. Binary measures are transparent and easy to replicate, but they discard variation within categories, and the transition years of different versions differ.

The Worldwide Governance Indicators aggregate dozens of perception-based sources into six dimensions: voice and accountability, political stability, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law and control of corruption. Each score comes with a standard error from an unobserved-components model. Coverage spans more than 200 economies from 1996 to 2025. A 2025 methodology revision tightened source selection, introduced a 0-100 scale and allowed the global average to move over time. The dimensions are highly intercorrelated (Langbein and Knack 2010), and their construct validity has been questioned (Thomas 2010), so use them as broad governance indicators rather than as measures of distinct concepts.

choosing: The most important choice is conceptual. Decide whether the theory requires a threshold (democracy versus autocracy), a degree (more or less democratic), a type (kinds of autocracy) or a process (episodes of change), and choose the family of measures accordingly. Within a family, measures differ less in their data than in their decision rules. Results that hold under one rule but not another reveal something about the mechanism, and they should be reported, not hidden.

Many measures are not independent. WGI incorporates commercial risk ratings and NGO assessments. UDS and the machine-learning democracy index are built from Polity, Freedom House and others. Episodes of Regime Transformation and Regimes of the World are functions of V-Dem indicators. Robustness checks that substitute one of these for its own source add little information. Where possible, pair an expert-coded measure with an observational or rule-based one, such as LIED or BMR.
gaps: Coverage of the most recent years is thin outside V-Dem, Freedom House and a few annual indices. Polity, GWF, UDS and most autocracy typologies stop between 2008 and 2018, which leaves recent autocratic consolidation poorly measured in typological terms.

Subnational regime and governance data remain scarce. Exceptions are the European Quality of Government Index, the Subnational Corruption Database, the U.S. State Democracy Index and State Reach in Africa. Subnational democracy in large federations outside Europe and the United States has no standard dataset in this catalog.

State capacity measures either cover a few dimensions with objective data (information capacity, census legibility) or rely on latent pooling of overlapping sources. There is no actively maintained, multi-dimensional, global series that extends beyond 2015 with uncertainty estimates.
Several commercial products (EIU, PRS, S&P Global, BMI) publish no reproducible methodology, and their histories are paywalled, which limits replication of studies that use them.
